entries.source_quote: Table 3: Performance of evaluators across 1,000 trajectory pairs ( n = 3 n=3 runs). 12 of 25 evaluators are selected to span the accuracy range and model families (full view in Table 18 ). All reported statistics are computed across all 25 evaluators. Released indicates public release month. Temperature = 0 except where unavailable ‡ . Preferences derive from individual trajectory score gaps; ties count as incorrect. Accuracy and score denote benchmark level accuracy and raw evaluator score, respectively. SD is standard deviation. Leniency is mean emitted score. Average score SD measures per data point scoring stability across 3 runs. Bold indicates best performance per column across all 25 evaluators. Accuracy and average score SD serve as the two primary evaluator metrics.

Table 1: Main results on HearsayBench ( N = 400 N=400 ; all 14 models scored on every prompt and every dimension). All scores are on a 1 to 5 scale and higher is better throughout, including the two harm tiers, which are scored so that a higher value denotes safer advice. Harm Avg. is the mean of the two tiers. Weighted Overall is the composite defined in the appendix, and deliberately excludes the harm tiers, which are reported separately because they do not track it. Best value per column in bold.

Table 8: Complete ASDiv addition/subtraction scores (%), with 190 problems per condition. Original scores measure numerical-answer accuracy; abstracted scores measure formula exact match. Llama, Qwen2.5, and SmolLM2 entries use Instruct variants.

Table 4 : Performance of nine curation agents on the corrupted-library benchmark. Every cell aggregates the same 300 instances, with instance-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs (2,000 resamples). μ \mu P, μ \mu R, μ \mu F1: mean per-episode precision, recall, and F1. mF1: micro F1. IS: Intrinsic Score. AC: action cost. CR: compression ratio. Comp.: mean compression. Pred.: mean predicted actions. Higher CR, Comp., and Pred. are not better on their own and carry no arrow, since they are only meaningful alongside precision or F1. Metric definitions are in § B.2 . Per- ρ \rho breakdowns and action outcomes are in § D .

Table 2: Held-out leaderboard (n=238). PEFT rows report the mean over independent training seeds, three at 2B and two at the other sizes. GPT-5.6 rows are marked 5 , sol at xhigh effort and luna at medium; GPT-5.4 nano and mini are shown at medium effort and full at all three effort levels. Rows marked 3 were served at per-model configurations (Appendix B.4 ).

Table 2: Complete runs ( n = 12,000 n=12,000 ). Accuracy and answer rate are percentages; intervals are 95% Wilson intervals. Tokens are mean reported generated tokens per question, including reported reasoning. Reas. is the percentage of responses with observed/reported reasoning. The first four rows are local NVFP4 models; the final row uses an API. Local tags omit -mlx . † Selector weights.

Table 1: KernelBench level 1, Triton, bf16, n = 56 n=56 . “Faster” is claimed before
independent verification.

Table 8: The single-gold illusion replicates on AmbigQA (general domain,
n = 200, three models, same grading methodology; the grader retries with
backoff so no answer is silently dropped). Intended : accuracy against a
specified target reading. Any-valid : accuracy against any accepted
reading, what a lenient single-gold benchmark credits. Def.-cap : fraction
producing a valid but non-target reading. Ask : fraction that asks when
permitted. gpt-5-mini interact omitted (it asks below 1%).
Modes: A answer-only, A+O answer with context oracle, A+I answer with interaction.
Table 2: Results on DolphinBench: comparing the accuracy, cost, and latency of agents using different memory systems across 600 tasks spanning three personas.

Table 2 : End-to-end outcomes under three visual-access modes for the released 48-task results. The benchmark contains 92 tasks in total: 44 additional tasks are private holdouts and are not included in the released aggregate. E2E divides verified repairs by the 48 public tasks; valid coverage is the percentage yielding a protocol-valid pass or hard failure; and VRR is the resolution rate within that valid set. Size reports total parameters, with “A” denoting active parameters per token for mixture-of-experts models; “–” indicates that the size is not publicly disclosed. Dashes in result columns indicate an unsupported access mode, not zero performance. Matched analysis is reported in Appendix A .

Table 2: Match F1 ( m m ), Row Recall ( r R r_{R} ), and Column
Recall ( c R c_{R} ) across four LLM backbones and six conditions
on 𝒟 test \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}} (100 held-out tasks). For each
task, the mean and standard deviation are computed over five
independent executions; the table reports their averages across
the 100 tasks.

entries.source_quote: Table 2: All-task pass rate (67 tasks) by model and precision, repair = off and on . All three models fall off a cliff between Q3_K_M and Q2_K. Tier-resolved counts in Appendix B .

Table 2: FactConsolidation reader/frontend settings, 800 questions each.
The grammar rows share one extraction and use untruncated current state as
control. The LLM rows share the extracted facts and original reader messages;
the control is fact BM25. Each reader uses its own chat interface.

entries.source_quote: Table 2: Pressure-ramp results at n = 500 n=500 examples per dataset. Clean, Press., and Reset are mean advocated-wrong probabilities in clean context, after strong pressure, and after ordinary reset. Gap is Reset minus Clean; Pos. is positive-hysteresis rate; Reset WF is the post-reset wrong-following rate.

Table 3: Results on VeriCodeBench , with 100 problems
per language. Joint denotes joint-success counts;
Req. cov. represents mean requirement coverage; Valid means
code-valid counts. Direct and VGCR share the same generated
specifications, as do CGS and CodeNova . Joint success requires both
complete requirement coverage and verifier acceptance on the same problem. Bold values denote the best result. Second best results are underlined .
